content_voiceover: This table is a high-yield comparison of the three major pediatric and adolescent liver malignancies, hepatoblastoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and the fibrolamellar variant of hepatocellular carcinoma, and the circled rows are the ones most likely to be tested. Age of presentation is a key discriminator, hepatoblastoma presents from birth to age three, hepatocellular carcinoma presents later, five to eighteen years, and fibrolamellar variant presents even later, ten to twenty years, often in adolescents and young adults without underlying liver disease. Associated congenital anomalies also separate them cleanly, hepatoblastoma is linked to dysmorphic features, hemihypertrophy, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma is linked to metabolic conditions like tyrosinemia or chronic hepatitis B, and fibrolamellar variant has no known associated anomalies, which is itself a distinguishing clue. A F P elevation follows a gradient, elevated in sixty to seventy percent of hepatoblastoma, fifty percent of conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, but only about ten percent of fibrolamellar variant, so a normal A F P in an adolescent liver mass should raise fibrolamellar variant on your differential rather than rule out malignancy. And the last circled row, abnormal vitamin B twelve binding protein, or transcobalamin, is essentially unique to fibrolamellar variant among these three, present in fibrolamellar but absent in the other two, making it a useful confirmatory marker when you're trying to distinguish fibrolamellar from conventional hepatocellular carcinoma.
keypoints: Age gradient: hepatoblastoma 0-3y, HCC 5-18y, fibrolamellar variant 10-20y
Associated anomalies: hepatoblastoma with Beckwith-Wiedemann/hemihypertrophy, HCC with metabolic disease, fibrolamellar with none
AFP elevated in 60-70% HB, 50% HCC, only about 10% fibrolamellar variant
Abnormal B12-binding protein (transcobalamin) is characteristic of fibrolamellar variant only
keypoint_voiceover: Use age to separate these three, hepatoblastoma under three years old, hepatocellular carcinoma five to eighteen, fibrolamellar variant ten to twenty. Hepatoblastoma links to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, while fibrolamellar variant has no associated anomalies, low AFP elevation around ten percent, and a distinctive abnormal vitamin B twelve binding protein that the other two lack.
